clue.text: Fugitive running Bond's race

indicators.note: something running is in motion and not standing still, so these letters move about into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A fugitive is on the run during a race involving James Bond.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a spy thriller chase; the anagram of the two words gives ABSCONDER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who absconds flees from custody or duty, which is exactly what a fugitive does.

clue.text: A long time taken up in scene of conflict

indicators.note: in a down entry, taking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
an era is a long period; with the article it becomes AN ERA, written here as the letters after A

explanation.surface: A long stretch of time is taken up in the setting of some battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A long time' together is AN ERA; read upwards in the grid it gives ARENA.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a place of contest, from Roman gladiatorial fights to any field of struggle.

clue.text: Homer, a simple chap, going round the outskirts of Paris

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps the other
the outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme simpleton
first and last letters of the city

explanation.surface: Homer, the poet, is pictured as a simple fellow wandering round the suburbs of Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Homer looks like the Greek poet, but it is the cartoon father; 'a simple chap' nods to the nursery rhyme Simple Simon.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer Simpson is the father in the long-running American cartoon sitcom The Simpsons.

clue.text: Proprietor getting some children worked up

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, the run of letters within them
in a down entry, going up means reading the letters from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A shop proprietor is getting some of the children excited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked up' reads as agitated; the 'up' alone is the reversal, so RENWO turns into OWNER.
explanation.definitionFit: A proprietor is the person who owns a business or property, so a synonym.

clue.text: Gallant in a hurry

blocks.note: first meaning: stylish and brave, attractively bold
second meaning: rushing along

explanation.walkthrough: The word is both an adjective for a dashing hero and the participle of a verb meaning to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallant figure is debonair and spirited, while someone rushing is literally darting about at speed.

clue.text: Where bandeau may be placed for supporter of Cromwell

blocks.note: first reading: a bandeau is a headband, so it goes encircling the skull, in two words
second reading: a Parliamentarian soldier in the English Civil War

explanation.surface: A headband's position is offered as a clue to someone who backed Cromwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as ROUND HEAD, it is where a band sits; as one word it is the nickname for Parliament's supporters, so called for their cropped hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundheads were the Puritan Parliamentarians led by Oliver Cromwell against the Royalist Cavaliers.

clue.text: Suffering with father at home

blocks.note: an informal word for dad
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Someone is in distress while their father is at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain is physical or emotional suffering, so the two words are synonyms here.

clue.text: Staff whip smelly animal

blocks.note: a staff is a long stick
the cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip

explanation.surface: Instructions to use a stick and whip to drive off a stinking creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Staff suggests employees and whip a verb, but both are objects here.
explanation.definitionFit: The polecat is a weasel-like mammal notorious for the foul-smelling secretion it releases.

clue.text: Dazed cook put on airs

indicators.note: to cook something is to work it over and change its form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A befuddled chef gives himself grand pretensions.
explanation.walkthrough: Cook looks like the noun for a chef, but it is a verb telling you to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a stupor is to be in a dazed, barely conscious state.

clue.text: Time runs out — it's the end of the line

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are not in their right order

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: As time runs out, someone announces that the train has reached the last stop.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is the final station on a railway or bus route, literally where the line stops.

clue.text: Hack Paul and do data transfer

indicators.note: to hack is to chop roughly, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to break into Paul's computer and move some data.
explanation.walkthrough: Hack plays on computer hacking, but it signals the mix; 'do' reads as a verb but is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An upload is the sending of a file from a local device to a server, a kind of transfer.

clue.text: German emperor in King Arthur's capital is seen by Her Majesty

indicators.note: a capital is the head or initial letter, so only the front of the word is used

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
the initial of the name
taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: A German emperor visits Camelot and is received by the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: King Arthur's capital suggests Camelot, but King and Arthur work separately. ER stands for Elizabetha Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaiser was the title of the German emperors, from the Latin Caesar, as with Wilhelm II.

clue.text: Show caught in country before half-term

indicators.note: one item placed in another is enclosed by it
only half of the word survives, so the rest of its letters are dropped

blocks.note: a large Asian country
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
taken as written before cutting

explanation.surface: A school display is caught in some country just before half-term holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-term looks like the school holiday, a short mid-term break in Britain; here it means half of the word term.
explanation.definitionFit: To indicate something is to point it out or show it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Little time at present for little fish

blocks.note: a minute, abbreviated
at the present moment

explanation.surface: There's only a moment to spare at present for catching tiny fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The minnow is a small freshwater fish, also used of any insignificant player.

clue.text: Train isn't diverted on the way

indicators.note: a diverted route is sent along a different path, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A rail passenger is told their train has not been rerouted on its journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods or people in transit are in the course of being carried from one place to another.

clue.text: They see people like Oscar Wilde holding German city up

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece encloses the other
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: wits are clever, amusing talkers, and Wilde was the most famous
an industrial city in the Ruhr

explanation.surface: Famous wits are said to hold a German city up, as if robbing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' suggests a robbery; here 'holding' encloses and 'up' reverses, as this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Witnesses are people who see an event, so 'they see' describes them as a plural noun.

clue.text: Have a meal with fruit brought round for primate

indicators.note: when something is brought round another, it encircles it

blocks.note: a fruit of the vine
to eat is to have a meal

explanation.surface: Someone dines and is brought some fruit to feed an ape.
explanation.definitionFit: The great apes, such as gorillas and chimpanzees, are a family of large primates.

clue.text: Ethel's at ground for sporty types

indicators.note: something ground is crushed into fragments, so these letters are broken and reformed

blocks.note: the letters of both words, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Ethel is at the sports ground, watching the sporty types.
explanation.walkthrough: Ground reads as a sports field, which fits the picture, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletes are people who compete in sport, so they are the sporty types of the clue.

clue.text: Conveniences on top of cathedral? Not exactly!

blocks.note: public conveniences are toilets
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Toilets perched on top of a cathedral? Not really!
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the first piece sits above the second; Ely is the crossword's standard cathedral city in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosely means in an imprecise, approximate way, the opposite of exactly.

clue.text: Extend term of imprisonment

blocks.note: first meaning: lengthen or draw out
second meaning: a prison sentence, in slang

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as lengthening a jail sentence; the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To stretch is to make longer, and a stretch is informal slang for a period served in prison.

clue.text: Run away from infertile area

blocks.note: first meaning: abandon
second meaning: a barren, arid region

explanation.walkthrough: A verb and a noun spelt the same but stressed differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert is to abandon a post, and a desert is barren land where little grows.

clue.text: Insect in secure US city

indicators.note: one item placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: secure means safe
a common insect

explanation.surface: An insect is lodged securely somewhere in an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Fe is the capital city of the US state of New Mexico.

clue.text: Wrecker rues boat wreck

indicators.note: to wreck something is to smash it apart, so the letters are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: The vandal regrets having wrecked a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A saboteur deliberately destroys or damages things, so is literally a wrecker.

clue.text: Notes, we hear, for singers

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of a word, not its spelling

blocks.note: tenners are ten-pound banknotes

explanation.surface: Banknotes are handed over to pay the singers.
explanation.walkthrough: Notes looks musical, which fits singers, but it means paper money; a tenner is a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenors are male singers with the highest natural adult male voice.

clue.text: Speed for musician or bad poet covering miles

indicators.note: something bad is faulty, so these letters are in the wrong order
to cover something here is to wrap around it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for miles

explanation.surface: A musician or a poor poet is pressed about pace over many miles.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled POET goes around M, which sits after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the musical term for the rate at which a piece is played.

clue.text: Dissolute men getting into scrapes?

definitions.note: a verb defining a plural noun, fair because rakes is also the verb form: he rakes means he scrapes

blocks.note: first meaning: libertines, men of loose morals
second meaning: drags a tool across a surface

explanation.surface: Libertines getting into trouble, as such men tend to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrapes reads as trouble, but here it is the verb: a gardener rakes leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Rakes are dissolute pleasure-seekers, and to rake is to scrape with a toothed tool.

clue.text: Fools before singular judge

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: Fools are paraded before a single judge.
explanation.walkthrough: Judge looks like a noun for a magistrate but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess is to evaluate or estimate, which is what one does when judging something.

clue.text: Hollywood star cheers when accepting award

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: cheers is an informal British thank-you
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: A film star is cheered as he accepts an award.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'cheers' is an everyday way of saying thank you, not only a toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Hanks is a two-time Oscar-winning Hollywood actor, known for Forrest Gump and Big.

clue.text: Don't go for support

blocks.note: first meaning: remain where you are
second meaning: a prop, rope or brace holding something up

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a plea to someone to stay for support; the two phrases are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To stay is to remain, and a stay is a brace or a rope steadying a ship's mast.

clue.text: Glasses needed when seeing ships?

blocks.note: first meaning: tall drinking glasses for sherry or beer
second meaning: fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessels

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether spectacles are needed to spot ships at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Glasses suggests spectacles or binoculars for seeing ships, but it means drinking vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is both a large drinking glass and a sailing ship with two or more masts.
